source.title: SCALAR: Benchmarking SAE Interaction Sparsity in Toy LLMs
source.authors: S. P. Fillingham; Andrew Gordon; P. Lai; Xavier Poncini; David Quarel; S. Heimersheim

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAE features as the basis for a benchmark of cross-layer interactions, but does not test the listed claims about superposition geometry, capacity pressure, polysemanticity, or SAE features as canonical model units.
record.gate_note: The reported results measure how SAE-to-SAE interaction ablations affect SCALAR scores. This is related to feature representations but is not a test of the claim versions listed. The human feature-interpretability assessment does not measure feature completeness, stability, or canonicity. The detached-gradient result concerns reuse between SAE feature chunks, not superposition geometry.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a benchmark (SCALAR) and a new SAE architecture (Staircase) and reports only how SAE architectures compare on cross-layer interaction sparsity. It uses SAEs as a tool. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity allocation, polysemanticity causes, distributed features, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Staircase (and Jacobian) SAEs achieve higher interaction sparsity than TopK under the relative SCALAR score, with absolute scores often favouring TopK. They report this in a 216K toy model and GPT-2 Small, without loss of individual feature interpretability (human raters near-evenly split, 348 vs 342 vs 310 indifferent).
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates a new SAE interaction-sparsity benchmark and Staircase SAE architecture; it does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported interaction-sparsity comparisons vary by SAE location and metric (absolute versus relative SCALAR). The GPT-2 Small evaluation uses down-sampled attributions and ablations on three prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Staircase SAEs lower relative SCALAR scores vs TopK (59.67% FF blocks, 63.15% transformer blocks, 38.69% GPT-2 Small), while absolute scores often favour TopK. JSAEs give an 8.54% aggregate gain across FF layers, with layer-dependent results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE architecture choices change measured cross-layer interaction sparsity; absolute and relative metrics can rank architectures differently.

fits_no_version.finding: In Staircase SAEs, active features at a layer are about 25–45% new and 55–75% reused from earlier layers (Figure 2). This concerns feature persistence across layers in the study's own architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many SAE features persist across residual-stream layers (pass-through features) when the architecture permits reuse.

record.problems: The main experiments use a 216K-parameter toy model. GPT-2 Small validation is down-sampled and uses three prompts at three block locations. Absolute and relative SCALAR results can disagree, and the JSAE coefficient is selected for minimum SCALAR score per layer.
record.rows_left_out: Raw SCALAR values and full ablation curves in Tables 7–11 and Figures 3, 10–14 are omitted where they duplicate the reported percentage comparisons. The detached-gradient chunk-use result (Appendix B, Figures 5–6) and the human feature-interpretability ratings (Section 4.5) are not rows for the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy superposition geometry, sparsity transition or feature-direction analysis.
All: no test of capacity competition or importance-based dimension allocation.
All: no analysis of polysemantic neurons.
All: SAEs are trained and used, but recovery of sparse features is assumed, not tested against an alternative.
All: completeness, splitting and absorption are cited as motivation only. The human interpretability ratings (Section 4.5) do not test canonicity or stability.
All: no test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: All rows compare the study's own or competing SAE architectures on a new benchmark. They bear on no version and should not count as tests. The conclusion mentions SAEs disentangling 'superimposed' features only as background motivation.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features exceeding network dimension are represented as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and whether geometry changes with sparsity.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions according to feature importance.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or are evidence for superposition.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or sparse features can be recovered with a dictionary.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of the model representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relation.reason: It uses sparse dictionary representations to compare circuit sparsity, without independently testing superposition or dictionary completeness, stability, or canonicality.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates SAE architectures using its interaction-sparsity benchmark; it does not test any listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: All sampled rows match the cited tables but are method comparisons, not claim-version evidence. GPT-2 aggregate relative reduction has inconsistent uncertainty within the paper: Section 4.4 gives 38.7 ± 1.2%, whereas Appendix J/Table 9 give 38.69 ± 0.71%, matching R33.
